pt>en:3b59ce98296c91f3: Delighting in the Trinity (Delighting in the Trinity, 2012)
pt>en:b1c32f6452748ebc: Fundamentalism and the Word of God (1958) and the Chicago Declaration on Inerrancy (1978)
pt>en:851c8205c68e9540: Reeves suggests a question: when you think of God, do you first think of a supreme power or of a Father who loves the Son? The answer shapes everything. The book's invitation is simple: to know the triune God and delight in Him.
pt>en:22df2a39d0a1cc36: Reeves starts from John 17:24, when Jesus speaks of the love the Father had for Him before the foundation of the world. Before any creature existed, God was already love: the Father loving the Son in the Spirit. A solitary god would need to create the world to have someone to love. The triune God creates not out of necessity, but out of overflow of love.
pt>en:21537f84556762ba: Michael Reeves, a British theologian, wrote a book with a bold proposal: to show that the Trinity is not a mathematical puzzle for theologians, but the heart of the Christian faith and the source of our joy. For him, who God is determines everything, including how we live.
pt>en:662c7fa2c6c56541: This changes the Christian life. Prayer is speaking with the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. Holiness is resembling the God who is love, and not just following rules. The mission of the church is the overflow of the same love that led the Father to send the Son. Even our joy in God is a gift of the Spirit, who pours that love into our hearts (Romans 5:5).
pt>en:8973063259adc2bb: For Augustine, studying God is not just an intellectual exercise. The goal is to love more the one we know. He says that our soul is like an image of God stained by sin, and that grace restores it as we contemplate God in Christ. Theology and worship walk together.
pt>en:7181481c1c6d8748: The Confessions begin with a phrase that has spanned the centuries: "You made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you." Augustine tells his own story of seeking pleasure, success, and wisdom, and concludes that none of this satisfies us, because we were created for something greater. Human restlessness is, at its core, longing for God.
pt>en:35580c0331017a11: Augustine's question applies: where has your heart sought rest? Work, approval, comfort, and entertainment promise peace, but do not sustain. The rest we seek has a name: the triune God who revealed Himself in Jesus Christ and invites us to return home.
pt>en:0e1d31e50f88b343: In The Trinity, Augustine seeks to understand, with reverence, how God is one and three. He starts from 1 John 4:8, "God is love," and observes that love presupposes someone who loves, someone who is loved, and the love itself that unites them. He himself acknowledges that no image is perfect, but reflection helps to see that the Trinity is not a cold enigma: it is the eternal communion of love of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.
pt>en:1ce4591739902801: In creation, the Father does all things through the Son and by the power of the Spirit. In salvation, the Father sends the Son, who gives Himself for us, and the Spirit unites us to Him. Reeves shows that salvation is being brought into this love that already existed. We are adopted to enjoy, as children, the fellowship that the Son has had with the Father since always.
pt>en:fd245289148b2818: Augustine, bishop of Hippo in North Africa, is one of the Church Fathers most cited by reformers. Calvin mentions him hundreds of times in the Institutes. Two of his works show how the doctrine of God touches life: the Confessions, a long autobiographical prayer, and The Trinity, a profound treatise on the triune God.
pt>en:338586ee74f5c467: In his great Reformed Dogmatics, Herman Bavinck devoted extensive pages to the doctrine of God. He reached a conclusion that marks all his theology: the Trinity is not an appendix of the Christian faith, but its living center. In his words, in summary, it is in the triune God that beats the heart of all revelation.
pt>en:817b48f4c0507e5c: Trinitarian faith changes the way we pray and live. We pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. We are called to live in communion, reflecting the God who is communion. And we await the day when we will see face to face the triune God, source of all joy.
pt>en:d033616a98939e95: One of Bavinck's most beautiful contributions is to show that God is not eternal solitude. In Him there is life, communion, and love from the beginning. That is why creation was not a necessity of God, but an overflow of His fullness. And that is why salvation is being included in this divine life as children.
pt>en:f7487e6a69b01f5d: Meek and humble: the heart of Christ
pt>en:7a39355717452987: Bavinck observes that all the great truths of faith depend on the Trinity. Creation is the work of the Father through the Son in the Spirit. Redemption is the Father sending the Son and the Spirit applying the work of the Son. If we remove the Trinity, the incarnation loses meaning, the cross loses value, and the indwelling of the Spirit becomes mere influence. Therefore, Bavinck says, the great errors in church history almost always began with deviations in God's doctrine.
pt>en:e79b9fa607ebcd02: Dane Ortlund wrote a book that surprised with its scope: a study on the heart of Christ that touched readers worldwide. The starting point is Matthew 11:29, the only place in the Gospels where Jesus describes His own heart: "I am meek and humble in heart."
pt>en:e1f570f5d2344c48: Bavinck is reverent. He states that the Trinity is a mystery that we cannot master with reason, but that we can know because God revealed Himself. It is not contradiction, because God is not one and three in the same sense: He is one in essence and three in persons. Theology, for Bavinck, begins and ends in worship.
pt>en:0158924ad55323de: The strongest application is for the Christian who stumbles repeatedly. Many imagine that Jesus grows tired of them, that there is a limit to divine patience. Ortlund shows the opposite: the believer's sin provokes in Christ not repulsion, but compassion. He not only forgives; he draws near. This does not diminish the seriousness of the sin; it increases the beauty of grace.
pt>en:0ba2275e6bd3e99d: If Jesus were not God, His death would not have infinite value. If He were not man, He could neither represent us nor have compassion for our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). Chalcedon and Anselm protect the same truth: our Savior is sufficient to save and close to comfort.
pt>en:28566301c17a389a: Ortlund notes that Jesus could have described himself in many ways: holy, powerful, just. And he is all of that. But when he opens his own heart, he says: meek and humble. It's not that Jesus doesn't have anger against sin; it's that his heart naturally leans toward the weary, the overwhelmed, and sinners.
pt>en:e044441745d54eb0: Anselm reasons thus: sin is an offense against the infinite honor of God, and humanity owes a satisfaction it cannot pay. Only God could pay, but only man should pay. Therefore, someone who was both God and man was necessary. The incarnation was not a detail; it was the only adequate response to the problem of sin. The reformers deepened this idea when speaking of penal substitution: Christ received in our place the punishment we deserved.
pt>en:4b6976156aecfc8a: Why did God become man? The question gives its title to a work by Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury in the eleventh century, and touches on the heart of the Christian faith. Centuries earlier, the Council of Chalcedon had precisely formulated who Jesus is. Together, Anselm and Chalcedon help to understand why the person of Christ matters so much.
pt>en:4efa5d7957bc79e9: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo, 1098) and Definition of Chalcedon (451)
pt>en:0f1e6bab6273b890: Matthew 11 ends with an invitation: "Come to me... and you will find rest." Ortlund asks the reader: how do you imagine Jesus looking at you at this moment? If the answer is disappointment, maybe it's time to let Jesus Himself correct that image.
pt>en:114845e5e79755cd: Next time you read the Gospels, notice both sides: Jesus tired, hungry, crying; and Jesus calming the storm, forgiving sins, raising the dead. It is the same person. And it is this person who intercedes for us today.
pt>en:1274cf50d5bbe67f: The Heart of Christ in Heaven with Sinners on Earth (1651)
pt>en:e67f5ea2d2d68da1: The Heart of Christ in Heaven
pt>en:3b3d289e7008aa79: In 451, the bishops gathered in Chalcedon affirmed that Jesus Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. These four denials protect the mystery: Jesus is not half God and half man, nor a special man adopted by God, nor God pretending to be man. He is fully God and fully man. The Definition of Chalcedon is in SOLA, in the creeds section.
pt>en:714b7d9db17f1350: The book dialogues extensively with the Puritans, especially Thomas Goodwin and Richard Sibbes. Goodwin wrote about the heart of Christ in heaven, showing that the ascension did not cool Jesus' love. Sibbes, in The Broken Reed, explores Isaiah 42:3: he does not crush the broken reed nor extinguish the smoldering wick. Ortlund brings these ancient works to today's reader.
pt>en:f38f99c86ab7eaf6: For those who feel far away
pt>en:5cd6a4c82ebb2c7c: Search: Thomas Goodwin The Heart of Christ
pt>en:c94d460a4ac565df: Goodwin analyzes Jesus' speeches in John 13 to 17, given on the eve of the cross. There Jesus promises not to leave the disciples orphaned, prepares a place for them, and prays for them. Goodwin sees in these words a window into what Jesus feels now. If he loved like that before going, he loves like that after arriving.
pt>en:3dee2467ad831cad: Dane Ortlund popularized this work in Meek and Humble, also in SOLA. Goodwin invites us to replace the image of a distant Christ with an intercessor Christ, who knows our name and bows down to us. Even today, he is praying for his own.
pt>en:c5abad9a30b32753: Thomas Goodwin, an English Puritan and one of the theologians of the Westminster Assembly, wrote a work with a long title and a simple question: after Jesus ascended to heaven and was glorified, does His heart remain the same with sinners? Or did glory make Him distant?
pt>en:7fe35c0c1970dd68: The ministry of the Spirit's spotlight
pt>en:c22d39d87422d1f8: A bold point from the book: Goodwin suggests that glory increased Christ's capacity to love, rather than diminishing it. He is freer and fuller to have compassion on His own. When a believer suffers or sins, Christ's heart moves toward him, to rescue and restore.
pt>en:6711b55d0a37fada: Goodwin answers firmly: the same. The Jesus who wept with Martha and Mary, who touched lepers and received sinners, is the Jesus who today is at the right hand of the Father. The ascension did not harden his heart. On the contrary, he remains human, with glorified human affections, and therefore sympathizes with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15).

pt>en:20249c50328aa352: For Packer, the greatest sign of the Spirit's presence is not the intensity of emotions nor the spectacular nature of the gifts, but holiness: the fruit of the Spirit described in Galatians 5, as love, joy, peace, patience, and self-control. He does not despise experiences; He only puts them in the right place. An experience that no longer produces love for Christ and more obedience must be examined.
pt>en:45f625b049efc284: Packer recalls what Jesus said about the Spirit: "He will glorify me" (John 16:14). A well-positioned spotlight illuminates a building at night, and no one looks at the lamp. That's how the Spirit is: it doesn't draw attention to itself, but points to Christ. Where Christ is exalted, known, and loved, there the Spirit is at work.
pt>en:9daf52c90b7954a4: The original title talks about keeping pace with the Spirit (Galatians 5:25). Packer describes the Christian life as a walk in which we follow the Spirit's guidance through the Word, prayer, and church fellowship. It is not passivity or activism, but humble cooperation: the Spirit works in us, and we work our salvation with fear and trembling (Philippians 2:12–13).
pt>en:86197d34df8faa1e: J. I. Packer wrote about the Holy Spirit at a time of much debate about gifts and experiences. Instead of entering only into controversy, he asked a deeper question: what is the central work of the Spirit? His answer became known by an image: the spotlight ministry.

pt>en:868c816ca05055d8: Christ outside of us, Christ within us
pt>en:df571e432f72ea31: The doctrine of union with Christ brings deep comfort: everything that belongs to Christ is yours, and you belong to Him. In times of weakness, remember: you are not just trying to imitate Jesus from afar; His Spirit lives in you and binds you to Him forever.
pt>en:fdd9a9702e9bb848: Sinclair Ferguson, a Scottish theologian, wrote one of the most comprehensive and pastoral studies on the Holy Spirit in the Reformed tradition. A central theme runs through the book: the main work of the Spirit in salvation is to unite us to Christ.
pt>en:7dc18573ed5881b9: A beautiful contribution of the book is to show the Spirit working in Jesus' own life: in the conception, baptism, temptations in the desert, miracles, the cross, and resurrection. The same Spirit that led Jesus in all his work is given to the church. That is why the Christian life is a life shaped in the image of the Son.
pt>en:ce01ffc9ddf8e5d3: Packer leaves a useful criterion for evaluating movements, worship, and experiences: Is Christ being magnified? Do people leave loving Jesus, His Word, and His people more? If so, the spotlight is on in the right place.
pt>en:0254662f45c012a1: The work of the Holy Spirit
pt>en:dc2c411840d85259: Calvin said that while Christ remains outside of us, everything He suffered and did for our salvation is useless to us. Ferguson develops this idea: the Spirit is the bond that unites us to Christ. Through faith, which is the gift of the Spirit, we receive everything that is in Christ: justification, adoption, sanctification, and the hope of glory.
pt>en:52116c03bb1653c9: Ferguson insists that sanctification is not a moral effort apart from grace. United to Christ, we die with him to sin and rise with him to new life (Romans 6). The Spirit applies this reality day after day. We fight against sin not to achieve union with Christ, but because we are already united to him.
pt>en:ed595451c21434e6: The Work of the Holy Spirit (Het werk van den Heiligen Geest, 1888)
pt>en:3364849c6023f152: The Spirit in the church and in the individual
pt>en:24e7c74bdd73bca9: Then, Kuyper describes the work of the Spirit in salvation: he inspired the Scriptures, formed the body of Christ in Mary's womb, anointed Jesus in his ministry, regenerates sinners, produces faith, unites the believer to Christ, and sanctifies him. Everything Christ has gained, the Spirit applies.
pt>en:07b5aa82232687b1: Kuyper balances the communal and personal dimensions. The Spirit dwells in the church as a temple and also in every believer. He distributes gifts for the edification of all and produces fruits of love and holiness. A spirituality that despises the church or ignores the heart is incomplete.
pt>en:bc90de730a949760: Kuyper begins before salvation. The Spirit hovered over the waters in creation (Genesis 1:2). He gives life, order, and beauty to the world. Kuyper attributes to the Spirit even the natural gifts: the skill of the craftsman, the talent of the artist, the wisdom of the ruler. Bezalel, who built the tabernacle, was filled with the Spirit to work with art (Exodus 31). This means that no honest work is outside God's interest.

pt>en:a3b000c7c4292938: Keller begins with the fact. The Christian faith does not rely on an abstract teaching, but on a historical event: the empty tomb and Jesus' appearances to many witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). He reminds us that if the resurrection did not happen, Christianity falls, as Paul himself admits. But if it did, everything changes.
pt>en:7c87d89c287b0fc2: Keller, in his last months of life, publicly said that illness had led him to believe in the resurrection in a more personal and real way than before. The book's invitation is the same: to let the resurrection cease to be just doctrine and become the hope that sustains today.
pt>en:b12f934b353f425c: The sky, a world of love
pt>en:280957526b3804c1: The resurrection of Jesus is the firstfruits of the harvest. It guarantees that those who are in it will also rise again. Keller insists that Christian hope is not to flee the world to a vacant heaven, but to wait for the renewal of all things: resurrected bodies, a new creation, full righteousness, and the presence of God among His people (Revelation 21).
pt>en:82a6aeab5da61901: Charity and Its Fruits, final sermon "Heaven Is a World of Love" (1738)
pt>en:4b74108ee80df257: Because of this, the Christian can face fear differently. Not denying pain, but knowing that death does not have the final word. Keller notes that the hope of resurrection has produced, throughout history, courageous Christians in caring for the sick, in the struggle for justice, and in faithfulness under persecution.
pt>en:484229c53c359450: Edwards starts from Paul's statement that love never ends (1 Corinthians 13:8). Faith will give way to vision, and hope to possession. But love remains and reaches perfection. That is why heaven can be described as the place where love is full: God's love poured out without limits and the love of the saints for one another, without envy, without pride, and without fear of losing.
pt>en:c77a6fac4b0aa638: The sermon ends with an appeal. If heaven is a world of love, whoever intends to get there must learn to love now. Edwards says that the Christian life is a journey toward that world, and that every act of true love is a taste of the homeland. Hell, by contrast, is a world without love. The question, then, is personal: is your heart being prepared for the place where only love dwells?
pt>en:742f58eaff6a4c1a: Edwards suggests something surprising: the joy of heaven will not be static. Since God is infinite, there will always be more to know and love. Eternity will not be boredom, but endless discovery.
pt>en:fc87e6a56c51ecee: Abraham Kuyper was a theologian, journalist, university founder, and prime minister of the Netherlands. Even with an intense political agenda, he wrote one of the most comprehensive treatises on the Holy Spirit in the Reformed tradition. Kuyper wanted to correct an oversight: many churches spoke of the Father and the Son, but almost nothing of the Spirit.
pt>en:392cd13ffa6b13b5: For Edwards, heaven is not beautiful because of golden streets, but because God is there, who is love. The Father, the Son, and the Spirit live in eternal communion, and the redeemed are brought into that love. Each one loves and is loved according to their ability, and all are satisfied, because no one desires what they do not have.
pt>en:0ee40f6757df4ff5: Tim Keller wrote Hope in Times of Fear during the pandemic while treating the cancer that would lead to his death in 2023. The theme is the resurrection of Jesus and what it means for those living in a world marked by fear and uncertainty. It is not a theoretical book: it is the hope of someone who looked at their own death.
pt>en:fd754c1ac42ad910: Kuyper's work broadens the perspective: the Spirit is present in worship and also in Monday work. Ask him not only for strength to pray, but for wisdom to work, creativity to serve, and love to live together. Every area of life is territory where the Spirit wants to act.
pt>en:75d0e21f5d91808d: Jonathan Edwards, pastor and theologian from New England, considered one of the greatest thinkers in American history, preached in 1738 a series of sermons on 1 Corinthians 13. The last of them has an unforgettable title: heaven is a world of love.
pt>en:cacde069617f746d: The Meaning of Marriage (2011), chapter on sexuality
pt>en:6e82d943902e09e4: John Bunyan was a poor tinsmith and Baptist preacher who spent twelve years imprisoned for preaching without a license. In prison, he wrote an allegory that became one of the most read books in history after the Bible: The Pilgrim. A Christian, the main character, leaves the City of Destruction and walks to the Heavenly City. The final scene is one of the most moving in Christian literature.
pt>en:8af5cf009465dde9: Sex as renewal of the alliance
pt>en:4cb6a9290e7a3bfe: The Pilgrim reminds us that we are strangers in this world, on the way to the homeland. It is worth asking: on what stretch of the path am I? And it is worth resting in the certainty of Hope: the riverbed is firm for those who are in Christ.
pt>en:83faedcecb72af1e: Grace for those who have already made mistakes
pt>en:bec8484d447ff280: On the other side, angels welcome the pilgrims, and they enter the city to the sound of trumpets. Bunyan describes the joy of those who arrive home. Death, for the believer, is not the end of the road, but the last crossing before glory.
pt>en:8fd24d3660730b9d: Upon approaching the Heavenly City, the pilgrim finds a deep river, without a bridge. It is the image of death. Christian is afraid and almost drowns, overwhelmed by memories of his sins. His companion, Hopeful, holds him and says he feels the depths, and that the depths are good. Then Christians remember Christ and the promise of Isaiah 43:2: when you pass through the waters, I will be with you. And cross over.
pt>en:ae7c0c69e0da19a9: Keller responds to common objections: "but we love each other" or "we need to know if we match." He argues that sex before commitment tends to create false intimacy, without the security of promise, and ends up teaching the person to protect themselves rather than surrender. Waiting is not repression; it is preparation for a complete surrender.
pt>en:df198649b4f16935: Keller's most well-known image is that sex is an act of renewing the covenant. In marriage, husband and wife made a public promise to belong to each other for life. In sexual relations, they say with the body what they promised with their mouth: "I am all yours, forever." Outside of marriage, the body says something that life is not saying. That is why the Bible reserves sex for marriage between a man and a woman.
pt>en:46498ec37980edc2: Before the end, the pilgrim passes through the Swamp of Discouragement, the Hill of Difficulty, the Valley of Humiliation, the Vanity Fair, and the Castle of Doubt. Bunyan portrays Christian life with realism: there are falls, temptations, and discouragements, but there are also faithful companions, shelter, and the cross, where the burden of guilt falls from the Christian's shoulders.
pt>en:b595f8549fafd05a: Keller begins by stating that the Bible is not against sex. It celebrates it, as seen in Song of Songs. Sex is good because it was created by God. But precisely because it is so powerful, it was given with a purpose: to unite two people entirely, body and soul, within a covenant.
pt>en:0ad7863de41d0bbe: In the book The Meaning of Marriage, Tim Keller dedicates an entire chapter to sex. He notes that the modern world treats sex as an appetite to be satisfied or as a form of personal expression, and that the Christian view is at once higher and more demanding.
pt>en:4c2a5cb1bd6bbc24: Keller also speaks to those who have lived differently. The gospel is not a court with no way out. In Christ there is complete forgiveness and a real new beginning. Purity is not just an untouched past, but a path that can be chosen today, by grace.
pt>en:23856426351c1d34: Sex and the supremacy of Christ
pt>en:13b2db1104ae163b: God made sex to reveal something
pt>en:44099c40ab37edc8: Sex and the Supremacy of Christ (org. com Justin Taylor, 2005)
pt>en:e68672558d350ac3: John Piper and Justin Taylor organized a book with lectures by various pastors on sexuality. The title sums up Piper's thesis: sex, like everything in life, exists for the glory of Christ. When Christ is the greatest treasure, sex finds its right place.
pt>en:ef6d1dc29e355630: For those who have already fallen, Piper reminds us that the cross is enough. Guilt doesn't have to be the last word. The same Christ who forgives is what gives strength to start over. Purity is the fruit of grace, not a trophy for those who never erred.
pt>en:c2c2452edf6e13f7: Piper argues that God created sexuality to teach us about it. The union of marriage is an image of the union between Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Conjugal fidelity shows the fidelity of Christ. Therefore, when sex is used outside God's design, He tells a lie about the gospel itself.
pt>en:0e420068332e60fe: Piper is realistic: sexual temptation is strong, especially in a world saturated with images. He does not offer tricks, but a strategy of faith. Sexual sin promises pleasure; the answer is not just to say "no," but to find greater pleasure in God. It is the logic he calls Christian hedonism: we fight against false pleasures with the promise of higher joys.
pt>en:041a72e8e2269291: Pure and Simple Christianity (Mere Christianity, 1952), chapter on sexual morality
pt>en:1a69f0c36404f115: Lewis makes an important observation: the sins of the flesh are serious, but not the worst. Pride, cruelty, and a cold spirit of judgment can be more dangerous. This protects against a hypocritical morality that condemns others and ignores one's own heart.
pt>en:daa2c7c3a9d5c23b: C. S. Lewis was not reformed. He was Anglican, a literature professor at Oxford and Cambridge, and author of The Chronicles of Narnia. But his chapter on sexual morality in Pure and Simple Christianity is cited by Christians of many traditions, including Reformed, for the clarity with which it addresses the subject.
pt>en:13fba66f3a275974: The Reformed tradition agrees with Lewis on the standard and adds emphasis on grace: we do not attain chastity only through effort, but through the work of the Spirit in those united to Christ. pt>en:ba9d49a658682a02: To illustrate, Lewis makes a famous comparison. Imagine a country where people fill theaters to see someone slowly lift the lid of a plate, showing a piece of meat.
